blocks.text: **6. Causes of Narrow Pulse Pressure (30-40 mmhg)**

items.text: Severe heart failure with low cardiac output.
Severe mitral stenosis with reduced stroke volume.
Septic shock (early or hyperdynamic phases may instead produce wide pulse pressure).
Radial artery compression or occlusion after arterial cannulation.
Aortic dissection involving the subclavian artery.
Severe hypothermia with marked peripheral vasoconstriction.
Marked oedema or local tissue injury obscuring the pulse.
Narrow QRS complexes in the absence of bundle branch block or pre-excitation.
Fine or coarse fibrillatory waves (f waves).
Ventricular response may be rapid, normal or slow.
Baseline may appear nearly flat in fine AF.
Possible ST–T changes secondary to rate-related demand ischaemia.
Possible pre-excitation with broad, irregular complexes in AF with an accessory pathway (e.g. Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome).

items.text: Assess stability: Airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs and ECG.
Haemodynamic instability attributable to AF: Immediate synchronised electrical cardioversion.
Digoxin in selected patients, particularly with heart failure or limited activity.
Avoid verapamil/diltiazem in significant systolic heart failure.
Antiarrhythmic drugs selected according to structural heart disease and comorbidities.
Assess thromboembolic risk using CHA₂DS₂-VASc or the locally recommended risk tool.
Assess bleeding risk and correct modifiable factors.
DOACs are generally preferred when suitable; warfarin is required for mechanical heart valves and moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis.

Before elective cardioversion: Assess AF duration and anticoagulation requirements; for AF lasting at least 48 hours or of unknown duration, use appropriate pre-cardioversion anticoagulation or an imaging-guided strategy, followed by anticoagulation for the recommended period.
Treat underlying causes: Infection, hyperthyroidism, electrolyte disturbances, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism and heart failure.
Investigations: ECG, electrolytes, renal function, thyroid function, echocardiography and other tests as indicated.
Special emergency: AF with pre-excitation/Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome — avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs; urgent specialist management is required.

subsections.subsection_title: 18. Management of Heart Failure — First, Second and Third Line

items.text: ARNI: sacubitril/valsartan; ACE inhibitor or ARB if unsuitable
Evidence-based beta-blocker: bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate
Loop diuretic: furosemide for congestion and fluid overload
Salt moderation, exercise/cardiac rehabilitation when stable, vaccination, adherence and daily weight monitoring

blocks.text: Second-line / add-on treatment for selected patients

items.text: Ivabradine: selected patients with HFrEF, sinus rhythm and persistently elevated heart rate despite maximally tolerated beta-blocker
Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate: selected patients intolerant of RAAS inhibitors or with persistent symptoms in appropriate populations
Digoxin: selected symptomatic patients or rate control in atrial fibrillation
IV iron: symptomatic HFrEF with documented iron deficiency, where indicated
Vericiguat: selected high-risk patients with worsening HFrEF despite guideline-directed therapy
Cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) in eligible patients
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) for eligible patients at risk of sudden cardiac death
Valve intervention for clinically significant valvular disease
Palliative and supportive care for advanced disease when appropriate
ABCDE assessment and oxygen only if hypoxaemic
IV nitrates in selected patients with adequate blood pressure, especially hypertensive pulmonary oedema
Treat precipitating causes: ACS, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled hypertension, pulmonary embolism, medication non-adherence
Non-invasive ventilation for severe respiratory distress when appropriate
Inotropes/vasopressors only for selected patients with cardiogenic shock or severe hypoperfusion under monitored care
Initiate and optimise the four foundational drug classes as tolerated.
Monitor blood pressure, renal function and potassium.
Avoid NSAIDs where possible, and avoid verapamil/diltiazem in HFrEF due to negative inotropic effects.
Do not initiate or up-titrate beta-blockers during uncontrolled cardiogenic shock or severe acute decompensation.
